claims.text: The proposed alloy has a density below 6 g/cm3.
The initial Mg-containing alloy is metastable and is either single-phase or mixed-phase.
Mg is initially distributed uniformly within the lightweight matrix.
Thermal aging can drive microstructural evolution in a high-entropy alloy.
Thermal activation causes Mg to diffuse out of the metastable matrix and segregate.
Segregated Mg forms discrete, stable Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates at phase or grain boundaries.
The Mg-rich intermetallic phases have a different chemical potential from the surrounding matrix.
Intermetallic precipitation or phase evolution can be associated with changes in high-temperature oxidation and corrosion behavior.
Mg-rich intermetallic regions modify the oxide scale through preferential MgO or mixed-oxide formation.
The oxide scales produced at the Mg-rich regions are more protective.
Electrochemical mismatch between Mg-rich intermetallics and the matrix creates localized galvanic cells.
The localized galvanic cells increase localized corrosion at intermetallic–matrix interfaces.
Aged samples will contain clearly segregated Mg-rich intermetallics relative to the initial state.
Aging will change high-temperature oxidation behavior, potentially yielding a thinner or more adherent oxide scale.
The proposed transformation requires a temperature high enough to activate Mg diffusion.
Insufficient Mg content may prevent the proposed transformation.
The corrosion and oxidation response depends on precipitate volume fraction, size, and distribution.
Failure to detect significant Mg segregation or Mg-rich intermetallic formation together with statistically indistinguishable oxidation and corrosion behavior would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The mechanism states that Mg-rich regions produce more protective oxide scales and induce localized galvanic corrosion, whereas the uncertainty field says whether the oxide is protective and whether galvanic cells accelerate localized corrosion remain uncertain.
